sections.html:
Frederick is the seat of Frederick County and the second-largest incorporated city in Maryland after Baltimore, about 46 miles west of Baltimore and roughly 50 miles north of Washington, D.C. The population was 78,171 in 2020, up from 65,239 in 2010, with 31,802 housing units and 5.8% of them vacant.

That growth means plenty of newer subdivisions on the edges and an older core downtown, where houses are far older than the rest of the stock. A downtown house can bring older wiring, plaster, small closets and stone or brick foundations. A buyer will price those in, and a cash buyer usually looks at the structure as is instead of asking you to modernize first.

Tax topicFiscal 2026 figure
Combined city and county rate$1.7134 per $100 of assessed value

The state reassessed Frederick County for January 1, 2026. Residential values rose 16.3% on average from January 1, 2023, phased in evenly across three years. If you are selling soon, check your latest state assessment notice, because the new phase-in amount affects the tax proration at closing.

The county mails annual and semi-annual bills in July and posts them online by July 1. Annual bills are due September 30. Semi-annual bills split into September 30 and December 31 installments. Interest starts October 1 at 1% per month on unpaid balances.

Paying in July earns a 1% discount and paying in August earns a 0.5% discount. The county Treasury Department is at 30 N. Market St., phone 301-600-1111. Each municipality levies its own tax, so ask Treasury before closing how the City of Frederick portion is billed and what the payoff will be.

The legislative services table lists no county transfer tax for Frederick County. The state's own transfer and recordation amounts still apply, so ask your title company for the exact closing figures before you set a net number for yourself.

If your house is inside Downtown Frederick's historic district, exterior changes need approval from the city's Historic Preservation Commission before work begins. All exterior alterations require approval unless they are on the minor rehabilitation list.

  • Sheds, fences, gates, walls and paving, including patios and driveways
  • Repair or replacement of doors and windows
  • Additions, porches, stoops, and outdoor HVAC or utility equipment
  • New lighting fixtures

Planning staff approve some projects, while larger ones go to a Commission hearing with a sign posted at the site. Call the city's Planning Department to find out whether your street is covered. Fixing up a historic house before listing can take longer than you expect, and a buyer who plans to renovate must account for the review. Selling as is skips that work for you.

sections.h2: Is flood risk a concern near Carroll Creek?
sections.html:
Parts of Frederick have a documented flood history. Carroll Creek Park began in the late 1970s as a flood control project after floods in 1972 and 1976, and it now serves as a downtown park with an amphitheater and pedestrian bridges.

Average annual precipitation is 43.52 inches, and heavy summer rain plus winter freezes can mean basement moisture, gutter problems and roof wear. Those are the first places a buyer's inspector will look. Check FEMA's flood map for your exact address and keep any flood insurance paperwork handy for the buyer.

Frederick sits at a junction of I-70, I-270, US 15, US 40 and US 340, with MD 80, MD 144 and MD 355 inside the area. Many people buy here for the commute to the Washington region, so a house near a ramp or a MARC station may draw different buyers from one on a quiet street.

MARC commuter rail runs to Washington, D.C., express bus route 991 goes to Shady Grove Metro, and TransIT runs local buses.

sections.h2: Do Frederick landlords need a rental license?
sections.html:
The city's rental licensing ordinance, approved in 2022, calls for a license at a fee of $120. It describes inspections of at least 15% of units each year, a free first inspection and fines up to $1,000 for operating unlicensed units.

If you rent out your house, call the city for the present rules and ask whether any license or inspection items are open before you sign a sale contract.

Most sellers of one-to-four unit homes in Maryland give the buyer either a condition disclosure or a disclaimer form. Hand it over before the contract is signed and keep a signed copy. A disclaimer sells the house as is, but known latent defects still have to be disclosed. If the form reaches the buyer late, the buyer has a right to cancel, so give it to them with the first draft of the contract.

sections.h2: Selling with deadlines, repairs or back taxes
sections.html:
Frederick sellers most often face one of three situations: an older downtown house with repairs and preservation rules, a rental that needs a license check, or a house in a family estate. Other points come up often.

  • A deadline to close before a move for work.
  • Deferred maintenance after years of renting.
  • Back taxes, liens or an unpaid water bill that must be cleared at settlement.

Your closing agent pays those items from your proceeds, so you do not need cash up front. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and approval, which can shorten the timeline when you are racing a deadline.

sections.h2: Closing day and what a cash sale skips
sections.html:
At settlement the title company collects the signed deed, pays the county tax balance and any liens from your proceeds, and sends you the rest. Bring photo ID, keys and any paperwork for repairs or flood insurance. Read the settlement statement before you sign and compare the tax proration with your latest bill.

A cash buyer has no lender, so there is no appraisal to fail and no loan approval to wait on. The buyer may still inspect the house and order a title search. For an older Frederick house with a long repair list, that often means a firm date and no negotiation over repair credits.

1. Ask Treasury for the current tax payoff and check your assessment notice. Do this first, because it sets the minimum your sale must cover.
  2. Find out whether your street falls inside the historic district.
  3. Confirm any rental license or inspection items with the city.
  4. Complete the Maryland disclosure or disclaimer form.
  5. Ask the title company for the closing figures, then close.

faqs.q: Is Frederick a good place to sell a house quickly?
faqs.a: Demand is supported by Fort Detrick, the county school system and biomedical employers, but your timeline depends on the condition and price. A cash sale can shorten it because the buyer does not need lender approval.

faqs.q: When are Frederick County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Annual bills are due September 30, and semi-annual bills are due September 30 and December 31. Interest of 1% per month starts October 1 on unpaid balances.

faqs.q: Do I need approval to repair my house in downtown Frederick?
faqs.a: If the house is in the historic district, exterior work generally needs Historic Preservation Commission approval unless it is on the minor rehabilitation list. Call the city Planning Department to check your address.

faqs.q: What is the combined property tax rate in the City of Frederick?
faqs.a: The fiscal 2026 combined rate is $1.7134 per $100 of assessed value. The county-wide rate alone is $1.1100.

faqs.q: How much did Frederick assessments go up?
faqs.a: Residential assessments in Frederick County rose 16.3% on average from January 1, 2023 to January 1, 2026. Increases are phased in over three years.
